extracted.subtask_description: Style and usage guidance for journalists reporting on race, ethnicity, religion, disability, immigration and related topics; provides preferred terms, words to avoid, capitalization, pronunciation and context guidance for news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: gypsy / gyp — avoid casual or pejorative use
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid casual use such as “they lived like gypsies, traveling from place to place” and the pejorative term gyp, (e.g. “I got gypped,”) which is likely derived from Gypsy and a negative stereotype of Roma people as swindlers and thieves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'gypsy' casually or the slur 'gyp.' Be aware of negative stereotypes of Roma people embedded in such usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: hadith — pronunciation and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “ha-DEETH.” A report or reports about a saying, action or tradition of Muhammad and his closest companions. Can be used as both a singular and a plural noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand hadith are viewed by Muslims as explanations of the Quran and are second only to Islam’s holy book as a source of guidance and Shariah. The two most reliable collections are by Bukhari and Muslim.

rubrics_metrics.name: describing Black/African American hair — ask and specify style
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a person’s hair in news stories, ask what style the hair is, don't assume. Black hair comes in a variety of styles and textures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific style terms (afro, bald/shaved distinction, braids/plaits, cornrows, dreadlocks/locks, extensions, Jheri curl, twists, weave). Avoid stereotyping; use hair details to open conversation or provide context only when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: hajj — pronunciation, meaning and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “hahj.” In Islam, a pilgrimage to Mecca ... It is the fifth of the Five Pillars of Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hajj takes place during the 12th month of the Islamic year; dates move because of the lunar calendar. The word hajj is typically not capitalized. A hajji is a person who has undertaken the pilgrimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: halakhah — pronunciation and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “ha-la-KHAH.” Jewish law, or the set of rules and practices that govern every aspect of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by Jewish scripture and teachings; interpreted by rabbis for each generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: halal — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arabic, something that is lawful and permitted in Islam. Halal refers to foods, objects and activities sanctioned by Islamic teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halal slaughter requires invoking God’s name and specific cutting to drain blood. Pork, blood, intoxicants and alcohol are not halal. Forbidden objects/activities are called haram.

rubrics_metrics.name: hamesh hand — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamesh is the Hebrew word for hamsa in Arabic. It means five or 'five fingers of the hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Jewish and Israeli culture the hamsa is often adorned with a Star of David or Hebrew letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: hamsa — origin and cultural use
rubrics_metrics.description: Often worn as jewelry, the hamsa is a non-religious, palm-shaped symbol for good luck or protection that pre-dates Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen in many cultures; some Muslims call it the 'hand of Fatima.' Arabic word hamsa means 'five.' Note cross-cultural adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: handicapped — avoid when describing people
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not describe a person as handicapped unless it is central to the story. Avoid using handicap and handicapped when describing a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the person's specific condition. Terms like handicapped parking may still be used when citing laws or places, though many prefer 'accessible parking.' Prefer person-first language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanukkah — preferred spelling and context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jewish Festival of Lights ... The eight-day holiday celebrates the Maccabees’ victory ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanukkah is the preferred spelling (Chanukah also common). For dates consult Jewish holidays resources like Hebcal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hapa — usage and historical note
rubrics_metrics.description: Once considered derogatory, hapa comes from Hawaiian phrase hapa haole meaning 'half white/foreigner.' It now describes anyone whose heritage is White plus another racial or ethnic group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is now considered by many a positive form of self-identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: haraam — pronunciation and meaning (forbidden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “ha-RAHM.” In Arabic, something that is forbidden or prohibited in Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when describing religious prohibitions; be accurate about meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: haram — pronunciation and meaning (sanctuary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “HAR-em.” In Arabic, a sanctuary or sacred territory in which all things are considered inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mecca and Medina have this designation. Distinct from 'haraam' (forbidden).

rubrics_metrics.name: hard of hearing — acceptable term, ask preference
rubrics_metrics.description: The term may be used to refer to people who have a mild to moderate hearing loss ... Those who are hard of hearing usually use speech to communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard of hearing is almost always acceptable, but use the term the person prefers. Deaf vs Deaf community affiliation affects preferred term. Use person preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haredi / Haredim — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hebrew term that literally means 'fear' or 'anxiety' and is used for devout believers who 'tremble in awe of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label can be applied to strictly observant Orthodox Jews instead of 'ultra-Orthodox,' but is not widely used outside Israel and Jewish media.

rubrics_metrics.name: HaShem — definition and reverent usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The word some Jews use in the place of the word God, which is considered too holy to utter. It literally means 'The Name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when appropriate; understand it's a reverent substitute for God's name in some Jewish contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasidism / Hasidic — definition and social structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A social and religious movement in Judaism founded in 18th-century Poland that stresses devotion in prayer and serving God in ecstasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hasidic Judaism is often structured around a 'rebbe' (revered spiritual teacher). 'Hasidic' is the adjectival form; followers are Hasidim.

rubrics_metrics.name: hate crime — federal definition and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the FBI, a hate crime is 'a traditional offense like murder, arson, or vandalism with an added element of bias.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For statistics, Congress defines hate crime as criminal offense motivated in whole or in part by bias against protected characteristics. Hate itself is not a crime; protect free speech and civil liberties in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hawaiian — ethnic identifier caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution. An ethnic group. Refers to a person who is of Polynesian descent. Unlike a term like Californian, Hawaiian should not be used for everyone living in Hawaii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Hawaiʻi resident' for people living in Hawaii who are not ethnically Hawaiian. See Pacific Islander.

rubrics_metrics.name: HBCUs — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically Black colleges and universities, established before 1964 to provide educational opportunities to people of African descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 100 institutions still exist; 'HBCU' is acceptable on second reference and in headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: hearing impaired / hearing impairment — avoid term
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms hearing impaired and hearing impairment are disliked by many because they describe a person in terms of a deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Federation of the Deaf considers 'hearing impaired' no longer acceptable. For total hearing loss, 'deaf' is acceptable; for partial loss, prefer 'partial hearing loss' or ask preference. Use person preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: henna / mehndi — definition and cultural note
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant used to make ink or hair dye. The ceremonial application of henna is called mehndi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indian women wear mehndi for special occasions such as weddings; designs fade after about a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: hermaphrodite — avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. Derogatory term for intersex individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'intersex' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: heteronormative / heteronormativity — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: These terms refer to the assumption that heterosexuality is the norm, which furthers the marginalization of queer people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to describe cultural assumptions and structures that privilege heterosexuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: heterosexism — definition and reporting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The attitude that heterosexuality is the only valid sexual orientation. Often takes the form of ignoring lesbians, gay men and bisexuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid erasing non-heterosexual people in coverage; use descriptive phrasing like 'LGBT right opponents' instead of 'homophobes' when describing opposition to LGBT rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: heterosexual — limited usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjective used to describe people whose enduring physical, romantic and/or emotional attraction is to people of the opposite sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 'straight.' Use as descriptive when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Holy Days — definition and dates
rubrics_metrics.description: The High Holy Days are the 10-day period beginning with Rosh Hashanah and ending with Yom Kippur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dates consult Jewish holiday resources such as Hebcal.

rubrics_metrics.name: hijab — definition and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally used to describe the scarf many Muslim women use to cover their head, but can also refer to modest dress in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wearing varies by region, class, sect and personal choice. Shiites more likely than Sunnis; women decide based on mosque, community and conscience. Avoid blanket assumptions; note diversity of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindi — definition and avoid confusion with Hindu
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary language of about 30 percent of India’s citizens, derived from Sanskrit using Devanagari script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse Hindi (language) with Hindu (religion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindu / Hinduism — definition and nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: India’s most popular religious and cultural system; oldest scriptures are the Vedas; broad spectrum of philosophies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hinduism can be described as monotheistic and henotheistic. Capitalize 'guru' before a name on first reference and use last name on second reference; 'Swami' is a title and should be capitalized before a name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindustan — caution on meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: This term once referred to a particular empire in northern India, but is sometimes used to refer generally to the Indian subcontinent or the Republic of India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of historical usage vs contemporary scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindustani — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An unofficial language spoken in northern India, a mixture of Urdu and Hindi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Indian languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: hip-hop / hip hop — definition and cultural scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Hip-hop is often identified as just a music form, but it goes well beyond music; includes deejaying, MCing/rapping, graffiti and breakdancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize hip-hop's cultural elements and global adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispanic — definition and regional preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: An umbrella term for people whose ethnic origin is in a Spanish-speaking country and U.S. residents/citizens with Latin American ancestry (not Brazil). Federal policy defines it as an ethnicity, not a race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term more common in Eastern U.S.; preferences vary regionally. U.S. Census uses 'Hispanic or Latino.' Provide context on preferences; see related entries like Latino/Latina/Latinx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispanic paradox — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show Hispanic communities may have higher risk factors for illness but longer life expectancy than non-Hispanics with similar health problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several studies attribute this to family cohesion; use carefully in reporting and explain factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hispaniola — geographic definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The large Caribbean island containing the Dominican Republic (east) and Haiti (west); name means 'Isle of Spain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct country distinctions when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hmong — definition and diaspora note
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethnic group living in southern China, Vietnam, Laos and Thailand; Laotian civil war in the mid-1970s led to an exodus to the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide appropriate background and avoid oversimplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hmong names — ordering convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name second, often one-syllable names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect naming conventions in reporting and identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holocaust — capitalization and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize when referring to the murder of 6 million Jews and others during World War II. Lowercase in other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to the term's genocide associations; consider alternative terms like Shoʾah in contexts where preferred. Historical context provided; consult Holocaust Memorial Museum for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy See — definition and distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A term of reverence for the Diocese of Rome; used to refer to the pope and his Curia when official church actions are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Holy See (entity) from the city-state of the Vatican.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Spirit — definition and preferred term
rubrics_metrics.description: The third entity of the Christian Trinity; once called the Holy Ghost, now Holy Spirit is preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Holy Spirit' as the preferred term in contemporary reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Thursday / Maundy Thursday — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The day before Good Friday when Jesus had the Last Supper; in the Catholic Church, Lent ends whenever the Holy Thursday service begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called Maundy Thursday; use appropriate term by context/denomination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Week — definition and components
rubrics_metrics.description: The week that begins with Palm Sunday and concludes with Easter Sunday; includes Holy Thursday and Good Friday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman Catholic Church sometimes uses 'Passion Week;' 'Holy Week' remains generally preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: homeless — person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who lacks a fixed, regular and adequate nighttime residence. Some prefer the term 'unhoused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ask which term people prefer. Use person-first language: 'people experiencing homelessness'; avoid 'homeless people' or 'the homeless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: homo — pejorative term
rubrics_metrics.description: Pejorative term for homosexual. Use only if there is a compelling reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid in reporting; use appropriate identity terms instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: homophobia — definition and restricted use
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear, hatred or dislike of homosexuality, gay men and lesbians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict to germane usage, such as in quotations or opinions. Use 'LGBT right opponents' or similar phrases when describing people who oppose LGBT rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: homosexual — limited contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun, a person attracted to same sex; as an adjective, relating to same-sex attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in medical contexts or when referring to sexual activity; prefer 'gay' or 'lesbian' in most other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hong Kong — political and historical note
rubrics_metrics.description: Former British colony, independent of Britain in 1997 and now a special administrative region of China under 'One Country, Two Systems.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of ongoing tensions about the meaning of that policy in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: hookah — see argilah
rubrics_metrics.description: See argilah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to main entry 'argilah' for usage guidance (not provided in this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: hujjaj — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers on a hajj pilgrimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct plural/singular form when describing pilgrims.

rubrics_metrics.name: humanist — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A rationalist who believes humanity is capable of morality and self-fulfillment without reliance on supernaturalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an accurate descriptor for secular philosophical positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: husband — acceptable but ask preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable term for a male, legally married partner of a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask which term the subject prefers when possible. See alternatives like lover, partner.

rubrics_metrics.name: hysteria — avoid pejorative use
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is sometimes used to describe people (especially women) as frenzied or overly emotional; historically linked to 'hystera' (uterus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term and related adjectives are pejorative and should be used with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: identify as / identifies a — avoid for trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the phrase 'identifies as' to write about a trans person’s gender when replacing it with 'is' doesn’t change meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Identifies as' can question a trans person’s gender by framing it as an identity rather than a statement. Use 'is' instead unless quoting a source. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: idol / murti — caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious in using 'idol' because it can imply a false god; do not use to refer to representations Hindus use in worshipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'murti' when referring to Hindu worship objects; avoid 'idol' and 'idol worship' as inaccurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: illegal alien — avoid; use alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. Alternative terms are 'undocumented worker' or 'undocumented immigrant.' Many find 'illegal alien' offensive and dehumanizing because it criminalizes the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'illegal alien' or 'alien' except in direct quotations. Note recent federal agency guidance moving away from 'alien' and similar terms (USCIS memo, Feb 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: illegal immigrant / illegal alien / illegals — avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid these terms when referring to immigration status. Use 'undocumented immigrant' or 'undocumented worker' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use 'illegal(s)' as a noun. Explain what immigration status means and avoid dehumanizing language. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: illegal / illegals — avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. Alternative terms are undocumented immigrant or undocumented worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term criminalizes the person rather than an act; avoid usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: imam — pronunciation and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'ee-MAHM.' In everyday use, any person in the Muslim community who leads a congregational prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally only men have been imams, but women can serve as imams for other women. In a formal sense, an imam can be a religious or political leader. Uppercase 'Imam' when preceding a proper name on first reference; on second reference use only the person's last name. Uppercase when referencing the Twelve Imams.

rubrics_metrics.name: immigrant — relevance and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioning that a person is a first-generation immigrant can provide background, but relevancy should be made apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss status of undocumented workers with sources and editors because of risk of deportation to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: implicit bias / unconscious bias — definition and remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes that unconsciously affect people's decisions and actions; often people are unaware of their bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit bias is harmful and important to discuss explicitly; institutions can interrupt it by adding steps to decision-making that consider racial impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: independent living — definition for seniors
rubrics_metrics.description: A housing arrangement for those aged 55+ who can live with little or no assistance; types vary from apartment-style to freestanding homes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These communities offer amenities and services; residents live independently but with easier navigation and less maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian Country — legal definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal term used in Title 18 U.S. Code that broadly defines federal and tribal jurisdiction in crimes affecting Indians on reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also used popularly to describe reservations and areas with Native American populations; use accurately in legal reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian languages — plurality and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: India has 14 officially recognized languages and many more fully developed languages and dialects; 29 languages had 1 million+ native speakers in 2001 census.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating languages as mere dialects; acknowledge diversity and regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian / Indian American — usage distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Indian' or 'person from India' for someone with ancestral ties to India. Use 'Indian American' for a U.S. permanent resident or citizen with ties to India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with 'American Indian' (indigenous peoples of the U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigenous — definition, capitalization and ownership language
rubrics_metrics.description: UN-based understanding includes self-identification, historical continuity, links to territories, distinct systems and languages. In U.S., tribal membership denotes Indigenous identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Indigenous identity as a proper noun; capitalize 'Indigenous' to avoid confusion with lowercase 'indigenous' describing plants/animals. Avoid phrasing that treats Indigenous people as possessions of states (use 'Indigenous people of Wyoming' not 'Wyoming's Indigenous people').

rubrics_metrics.name: indigenous religion — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to myriad local and regional religious traditions shaped by language, kinship, mythologies and rituals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize uniqueness and local variations; do not conflate with major world religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indo — modifier usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A modifier used to denote something of Indian origin or with an India connection; similar to 'Sino' for China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Indo-U.S. relations'; term increasingly used for South Asian diaspora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indochina — caution on geographic scope and connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, but not nearby Thailand and Burma (Myanmar). Some say the term has a colonialist connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution and be precise about countries included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indonesian names — naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Indonesians have two names, but having only one name is also common. Muslims have complex name rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect local naming customs when identifying people.

rubrics_metrics.name: infantile paralysis — prefer 'polio'
rubrics_metrics.description: Infantile paralysis is short for poliomyelitis and was commonly used in the past to describe polio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'polio' rather than 'infantile paralysis.' Prefer phrasing like 'He had polio as a child' rather than 'He suffers from polio' or 'He is a victim of polio.'

rubrics_metrics.name: injury / injuries — preferred verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Injury describes harm resulting from an accident or event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to injuries as 'sustained' or 'received,' not 'suffered,' unless subject prefers 'suffered.'

rubrics_metrics.name: inmate — avoid when referring to people
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid this term when referring to a person who is incarcerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructions including 'person' or 'people' and biographical details: 'incarcerated people,' 'imprisoned people,' 'people in prison,' 'people in jail,' 'formerly incarcerated people,' or named examples with facility context.

rubrics_metrics.name: inner city — avoid euphemistic racial connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'inner city' has been used as a euphemism for lower-income residential districts, sometimes referring to Black neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'city center,' 'downtown' or 'central urban' for neighborhoods; use 'under-resourced' or 'low-income' when referring to poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane asylum / mental health hospital / psychiatric hospital — preferred terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospitals once commonly called insane asylums are now referred to as mental health hospitals or psychiatric hospitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'mental health hospital' or 'psychiatric hospital' as accurate and non-stigmatizing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane / incompetent — avoid pejorative use; prefer clinical/legal terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like insane, insanity and mentally deranged are offensive and informal; medical profession favors 'mental disorder' or 'psychopathology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'mental illness' or 'mental disorder' instead, except in quotes or when referring to a legal 'insanity' defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: inscrutable — caution about racialized connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Synonym for mysterious, but considered a racially charged adjective, particularly when used to describe Asians or Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'inscrutable' to describe people from racial/ethnic groups where it may be charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: institutional racism — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When policies and practices put people who are not of the dominant race at a disadvantage; occurs across institutions like government, business, education and media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that institutional racism can be structural rather than intentional. Provide examples such as housing policies or school discipline systems ('school-to-prison pipeline'). See related terms: systemic racism, White privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: intellectual disability — definition and person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: A disability involving significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior; often defined by AAIDD with IQ thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use person-first language: 'person with an intellectual disability' rather than 'intellectually disabled.' Note typical developmental timing (before age 18).

rubrics_metrics.name: intelligent design — definition and context
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that some aspects of life forms are so complex they must reflect the design of a conscious intelligence; proponents often imply God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize in debates about evolution and creationism; identify as a belief rather than settled science.

rubrics_metrics.name: interdenominational — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A congregation or organization formally approved or under the jurisdiction of more than one denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a synonym for 'nondenominational.' Use precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: interfaith — definition and distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to activities or events that draw people from entirely different religious traditions (e.g., Christians, Jews, Buddhists and Muslims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a synonym for 'ecumenical,' which refers to a multiplicity of Christian traditions; use precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: internment, Japanese — historical definition
rubrics_metrics.description: During WWII, the incarceration of 120,000 men, women and children of Japanese ancestry, two-thirds U.S. citizens; they were ordered to sell homes/businesses and move to 'relocation centers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note historical context and consequences when reporting; last internees released in 1946.
